hook: A family in Detroit may live a mile from a dollar store full of chips and soda but several miles from the nearest supermarket selling fresh vegetables. Meanwhile a farm 50 km away sells boxes of produce to members who paid in spring. Feeding people well is as much about access as about growing food.

prereq.q: When did GMO crops first reach farms?
prereq.why: GMO crops came after the Green Revolution, in the late 1990s.

prereq.q: What does a global supply chain include?
options: Every step and place from farm to consumer, across countries
Just the ships that carry food
Just the farms that grow food
Just the stores that sell food
prereq.why: A supply chain is every step: growing, processing, shipping, storing and selling.

figure.caption: Neighborhood N lies outside the 1-mile circle around the town's only supermarket.

chain.cause: A neighborhood has no supermarket within a mile, and many families have low incomes and no car
chain.effect: people buy much of their food at corner stores

chain.cause: Corner stores sell little fresh food
chain.effect: families eat fewer fruits and vegetables

chain.cause: Residents start urban farms and a farmers market
chain.effect: fresh food becomes easier to get close to home

ideas: Debates: GMOs (reviews found them safe to eat; critics cite seed patents, resistant weeds and control by a few firms) and aquaculture (food and income, but some habitat loss and pollution).
Food-choice movements: organic, local food, community-supported agriculture, urban farming, value-added specialty crops, fair trade and dietary shifts.
Food insecurity comes mostly from poverty, conflict, poor distribution and bad weather; a food desert is an area with poor access to affordable, healthy food.

misconception.wrong: People go hungry because the world does not grow enough food.
misconception.right: The world grows enough calories. Hunger comes mostly from poverty, conflict, poor distribution and bad weather that keep food from people.

summary: Farming faces debates over GMOs and aquaculture, and shoppers drive movements such as organic, local food, CSA, urban farming, value-added crops and fair trade. Food insecurity and food deserts come mostly from poverty, conflict, distribution, weather and lost farmland, not from too little food.
